title: 2 Kings 11:1–16
context: After Jehu kills King Ahaziah of Judah (9:27), Ahaziah’s mother Athaliah, of the house of Ahab and Omri (8:18, 26), seizes power and sets out to destroy the royal family of Judah. Jehosheba, Ahaziah’s sister, rescues the infant Joash and hides him with his nurse, and he stays hidden in the LORD’s house for six years while Athaliah reigns. In the seventh year Jehoiada the priest makes a covenant with the commanders of the guard, shows them the king’s son, and arranges guards around the temple and the boy. He arms them with David’s spears and shields, crowns Joash, gives him the covenant, and has him anointed while the people acclaim him. Athaliah comes, cries treason, and is taken out of the temple precincts and put to death. The parallel account in 2 Chronicles 22:10–23:15 adds that Jehosheba (there Jehoshabeath) was Jehoiada’s wife. The narrative is told with restraint. Both traditions read it as shared ground: the LORD preserved David’s line as he had promised (2 Samuel 7:12–16; compare 2 Kings 8:19), working through the courage of a woman, a priest and loyal guards.

verses.text: Now when Athaliah the mother of Ahaziah saw that her son was dead, she arose and destroyed all the royal offspring.
verses.arminianNotes:
When Athaliah, Ahaziah’s mother, sees that her son is dead, she sets out to destroy the whole royal family. The narrator reports this in a single sober sentence.

Arminian readers note that Athaliah’s act is her own deliberate and grievous choice, driven by ambition, and that Scripture records such evil honestly without suggesting that God approved it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that Athaliah’s attempt threatened the line through which God had promised to keep a lamp for David (8:19), so the story that follows shows God preserving his promise even when it seemed nearly extinguished.

Both traditions read the verse with sorrow and hold Athaliah responsible for the violence she ordered.

verses.text: But Jehosheba, the daughter of King Joram, sister of Ahaziah, took Joash the son of Ahaziah, and stole him away from among the king’s sons who were slain, even him and his nurse, and put them in the bedroom; and they hid him from Athaliah, so that he was not slain.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehosheba, daughter of King Joram and sister of Ahaziah, takes the infant Joash from among the king’s sons who are being killed and hides him with his nurse in a bedroom. She saves his life.

Arminian readers note that Jehosheba acts courageously and at great personal risk, and that God’s purposes advance through the free and faithful choices of ordinary people willing to act.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s providence preserves David’s line through the hidden act of one woman, and that the parallel in 2 Chronicles 22:11 identifies her as the wife of Jehoiada the priest, linking the rescue to the priestly household.

Both traditions honor Jehosheba’s courage and see God’s faithfulness at work through her.

verses.text: He was with her hidden in the LORD’s house six years while Athaliah reigned over the land.
verses.arminianNotes:
Joash stays hidden with her in the LORD’s house for six years while Athaliah reigns over the land. The rightful heir grows up in hiding.

Arminian readers note that the six years of waiting required sustained faithfulness from those who protected the child, showing that obedience to God often involves patience and quiet perseverance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God sheltered the heir of David in his own house, an image of the LORD guarding his promise in the place where his name dwelt, even while a usurper ruled outside.

Both traditions read the hidden years as shared ground: the LORD kept his promise to David even in a dark time, and he used human faithfulness to do it.

verses.text: In the seventh year Jehoiada sent and fetched the captains over hundreds of the Carites and of the guard, and brought them to him into the LORD’s house; and he made a covenant with them, and made a covenant with them in the LORD’s house, and showed them the king’s son.
verses.arminianNotes:
In the seventh year, Jehoiada sends for the commanders of the Carites and the guard, brings them into the LORD’s house, makes a covenant with them, and shows them the king’s son. The Carites were probably royal guards; their identity is uncertain.

Arminian readers note that Jehoiada wisely seeks the willing commitment of the guards, binding them by covenant rather than compelling them.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the revelation of the king’s son in the LORD’s house marks the turning point of God’s plan to restore the Davidic line, and that the covenant binds the participants before the LORD.

Both traditions see Jehoiada’s leadership as faithful and see the covenant as rooted in loyalty to God’s promise.

verses.text: He commanded them, saying, “This is what you must do: a third of you, who come in on the Sabbath, shall be keepers of the watch of the king’s house;
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoiada commands that a third of those coming on duty on the Sabbath guard the king’s house. He begins to give detailed instructions.

Arminian readers note that Jehoiada’s careful planning shows that trust in God’s promises does not exclude prudence, and that faithful people use wisdom and organization in serving God’s purposes.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the use of the Sabbath change of guard allowed both outgoing and incoming companies to be present without drawing attention, an example of how God’s purposes are served through ordinary means and careful timing.

Both traditions read the instructions as practical wisdom in the service of restoring the rightful king.

verses.text: a third of you shall be at the gate Sur; and a third of you at the gate behind the guard. So you shall keep the watch of the house, and be a barrier.
verses.arminianNotes:
A third are to be at the gate Sur, and a third at the gate behind the guard, keeping watch over the house as a barrier. The parallel in 2 Chronicles 23:5 names a gate of the foundation.

Arminian readers note that the precise locations of these gates are uncertain, and that the narrative’s point is the careful protection of the young king rather than a map of the temple area.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the guards form a protective barrier around the place where the king will be revealed, emphasizing the seriousness with which the restoration of David’s line was undertaken and guarded.

Both traditions hold the details of the gates lightly and read the verse as narrative.

verses.text: The two companies of you, even all who go out on the Sabbath, shall keep the watch of the LORD’s house around the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
The two companies going off duty on the Sabbath are to guard the LORD’s house around the king. The guard is doubled.

Arminian readers note that Jehoiada mobilizes all available forces, showing the importance of the moment and the willingness of the guards to commit fully to the plan.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the king is surrounded by guards within the LORD’s house, so that the restoration of David’s heir takes place under the protection of God’s house and his people, a fitting setting for the renewal of the covenant.

Both traditions read the arrangement as a careful and faithful plan to protect the young king.

verses.text: You shall surround the king, every man with his weapons in his hand; and he who comes within the ranks, let him be slain. Be with the king when he goes out, and when he comes in.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The guards are to surround the king with weapons in hand, killing anyone who breaks through the ranks, and staying with the king wherever he goes. The orders are firm.

Arminian readers note that the use of force here is defensive, aimed at protecting the rightful king from those who would harm him, and that the text reports these orders without glorifying violence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the guarding of the king’s person reflects the high stakes of the moment, since the survival of David’s line was at risk, and that the narrative presents Jehoiada’s measures as fitting for that crisis.

Both traditions read the orders soberly as part of the narrative of restoration.

verses.text: The captains over hundreds did according to all that Jehoiada the priest commanded; and they each took his men, those who were to come in on the Sabbath with those who were to go out on the Sabbath, and came to Jehoiada the priest.
verses.arminianNotes:
The commanders do everything Jehoiada the priest commands, each bringing his men, those coming on and those going off duty on the Sabbath. Obedience is complete.

Arminian readers note that the commanders freely join the plan and carry it out fully, showing how willing cooperation among God’s people can accomplish what no single person could.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the unity of the commanders under the priest’s direction is part of God’s providential ordering of events to restore David’s heir, working through human loyalty and obedience.

Both traditions see the commanders’ obedience as faithful participation in God’s purpose.

verses.text: The priest delivered to the captains over hundreds the spears and shields that had been King David’s, which were in the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
The priest gives the commanders the spears and shields that had belonged to King David, which were kept in the LORD’s house. David’s weapons arm the guards.

Arminian readers note that the use of David’s own weapons connects the restoration with the founder of the dynasty, reminding the people of God’s promise to David.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that David’s weapons in the hands of the guards symbolize the continuity of God’s covenant with David, as the king God promised to establish is now protected with the arms of his ancestor (2 Samuel 7:16).

Both traditions see this detail as a reminder that the restoration is the fulfillment of God’s promise to David.

verses.text: The guard stood, every man with his weapons in his hand, from the right side of the house to the left side of the house, along by the altar and the house, around the king.
verses.arminianNotes:
The guards stand with weapons in hand from the right side of the house to the left, by the altar and the house, around the king. The king is fully protected.

Arminian readers note that the careful positioning of the guards around the altar and the house shows that the restoration takes place in the presence of God, and that the whole community is involved in protecting the king.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the king is surrounded in the place of worship, near the altar, which signals that his reign is meant to be under God’s authority and connected to the true worship of the LORD.

Both traditions read the scene as the careful protection of God’s chosen king in God’s house.

verses.text: Then he brought out the king’s son, and put the crown on him, and gave him the covenant; and they made him king and anointed him; and they clapped their hands, and said, “Long live the king!”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoiada brings out the king’s son, puts the crown on him, gives him the covenant, and they make him king and anoint him; they clap and shout for the king to live. The coronation is joyful.

Arminian readers note that the people’s acclamation is a willing response to God’s provision, and that the giving of the covenant, perhaps a copy of the law (compare Deuteronomy 17:18–19), calls the king to obedience.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the word rendered covenant may refer to a document of testimony, and its precise nature is debated; either way, the king is installed under God’s word.

Both traditions see the crowning of Joash as the visible fulfillment of God’s faithfulness to David’s line.

verses.text: When Athaliah heard the noise of the guard and of the people, she came to the people into the LORD’s house;
verses.arminianNotes:
When Athaliah hears the noise of the guard and the people, she comes to the people at the LORD’s house. She is drawn by the sound.

Arminian readers note that Athaliah comes unaware of what has happened, and that the noise of rejoicing exposes her usurpation, showing that hidden purposes of God come to light in his time.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the usurper comes to the very house where God had hidden the heir, so that God’s providence brings her face to face with the failure of her plan.

Both traditions read the verse as the moment when Athaliah’s attempt to destroy David’s line is shown to have failed.

verses.text: and she looked, and behold, the king stood by the pillar, as the tradition was, with the captains and the trumpets by the king; and all the people of the land rejoiced, and blew trumpets. Then Athaliah tore her clothes and cried, “Treason! Treason!”
verses.arminianNotes:
She sees the king standing by the pillar, as was the custom, with the commanders and trumpeters, and all the people rejoicing and blowing trumpets; she tears her clothes and cries treason. The scene is reversed.

Arminian readers note that Athaliah’s cry is ironic, since she herself had seized power by violence, and that sin often accuses others of what it has done.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the king standing by the pillar, as was customary for kings (compare 23:3), signals his legitimate place, and that the rejoicing of the people of the land confirms that God has restored the rightful line.

Both traditions read the verse as narrative of a usurper exposed and a rightful king restored.

verses.text: Jehoiada the priest commanded the captains of hundreds who were set over the army, and said to them, “Bring her out between the ranks. Kill anyone who follows her with the sword.” For the priest said, “Don’t let her be slain in the LORD’s house.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jehoiada orders the commanders to bring her out between the ranks and to kill anyone who follows her, for she must not be killed in the LORD’s house. The priest protects the sanctity of the temple.

Arminian readers note that Jehoiada’s concern for the holiness of the LORD’s house shows reverence even in a moment of crisis.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that the instruction to remove her from the temple precincts reflects concern that the LORD’s house not be defiled by bloodshed, and that the narrative presents her death as a judicial act rather than mob violence.

Both traditions read the verse soberly and note the care taken to respect the holiness of God’s house.

verses.text: So they seized her; and she went by the way of the horses’ entry to the king’s house, and she was slain there.
verses.arminianNotes:
They seize her, and she goes by the way of the horses’ entrance to the king’s house, and she is put to death there. The narrator reports her death briefly.

Arminian readers note that the narrative does not dwell on the violence, and that Athaliah’s end is the consequence of her own murderous seizure of power, a sober reminder that evil brings judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers note that God’s justice falls on the one who tried to destroy David’s line, and that the brevity of the account keeps the focus on God’s faithfulness rather than on the details of her death.

Both traditions read her death as just judgment and handle it without sensationalism.
